## Frequently asked questions

### Who is Somesh Mohapatra?

Somesh Mohapatra, PhD, MBA, is an AI, data science and product leader. He is Director of Analytics at Caterpillar Inc., where his teams build digital twins and agentic AI for global manufacturing. He holds a PhD in machine learning for molecular design from MIT and an MBA from MIT Sloan's Leaders for Global Operations program.

### What does Somesh Mohapatra do at Caterpillar?

He is Director of Analytics and Head of Data Science and Product Management for Caterpillar's Modern Manufacturing digital platform, covering predictive maintenance, inventory, dynamic scheduling, connected assets and operational metrics across 150+ facilities. Earlier at Caterpillar he was chief of staff for strategy in the $15B Resource Industries segment, led minesite electrification analytics, and built ChatDocs, a GenAI platform for supplier contracts that earned the CEO Award.

### How large are the teams and programs Somesh Mohapatra has led?

He is accountable for a 100+ person organization as a leader of leaders, with nine direct reports and managers of data scientists, AI and GenAI engineers, simulation developers and product managers across the US and India, and owns the AI and product roadmap for a manufacturing digital platform scoped to 150+ facilities; the platform program runs on a $30M annual budget. Earlier at Caterpillar he co-led a supply resiliency program covering 1.5 million parts, 7,000+ suppliers and $20B of annual spend, and did strategy and capital-allocation work for the $15B Resource Industries segment. As a startup co-founder he grew a team from two to 30 people with full P&L ownership.

### Where did Somesh Mohapatra study?

He earned a PhD in machine learning for molecular design at MIT, advised by Prof. Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli, a dual-degree MBA from the MIT Sloan Leaders for Global Operations program, and a B.Tech from IIT Roorkee, where he won the Institute Gold Medal as rank 1 of 110.

### What is Somesh Mohapatra's research about?

His research applies machine learning to molecules, materials and manufacturing: graph representations of macromolecules (GLAMOUR), deep learning for peptide design and fast-flow peptide synthesis, and reaction impurity prediction for drug manufacturing. He has 15+ peer-reviewed papers, including two in Nature Chemistry and several in ACS Central Science, and a US patent application on AI-designed drug delivery peptides.

### How does Somesh Mohapatra approach enterprise AI?

His playbook treats data and AI as a multiplier for the business a company already wants to become: start from the business's core learning problem, fix data foundations before models, run one governed AI platform with risk-tiered governance, grant agents autonomy per workflow, and measure decisions changed and value created rather than pilots launched.

### What does Somesh Mohapatra speak and write about?

He writes and speaks about enterprise AI, digital twins, agentic systems and AI in manufacturing, supply chain and operations, through his LinkedIn essay series, invited talks and his playbook on data and AI at scale. He is always glad to compare notes with practitioners, researchers and leaders working on the same problems.

### What is Somesh Mohapatra building and writing about now?

He builds in the open on GitHub (github.com/pikulsomesh): browser-based digital twins, spatial AI that turns a walkthrough video into an OpenUSD twin, developmental world models and on-device AI. He writes weekly on LinkedIn about open-weight models, inference economics, agent design and evaluation, and what AI does to work, teams and judgment.

### Where is Somesh Mohapatra based, and how can I contact him?

He is based in the Dallas–Fort Worth area of Texas and works across the US, UK and India. The best ways to reach him are email (from the contact section of someshmohapatra.in) or LinkedIn at linkedin.com/in/pikulsomesh.

## Recent builds

- Food Bank Spatial Twin (Spatial AI; Live): Digital twins usually start from CAD drawings and laser scans, which puts them out of reach for most non-profits. Is a public video tour enough to start one? Frames of a public news tour of a food bank become Gaussian-splat captures through a world model, a scripted Blender model fills in the parts the video never showed, and OpenUSD ties both to operations data served from a serverless AWS backend. The twin runs in the browser and in NVIDIA Omniverse on EC2 GPUs. Built in seven days for about $1.54 of compute, with a reference architecture mapped to AWS, Azure and Google Cloud and real sensors priced at about $12 a month to run. Stack: World model API, 3D Gaussian splatting, Blender, OpenUSD, AWS SAM + Lambda, Omniverse on EC2, three.js. https://pikulsomesh.github.io/foodbank-spatial-twin/
- Michelin Kitchen Twin (Digital twin; Live): Factory planning ideas like MRP, routings and OEE are hard to show with plant data nobody can share. A famous kitchen makes them visible to anyone. A 3D twin of a three-star kitchen running a full tasting-menu service. Covers are the build plan, 53 recipes are bills of materials and routings, and a discrete-event simulation plays out tickets, stations and bottlenecks minute by minute. Parallel coding agents built the product, data, simulation and 3D layers. Stack: three.js, Discrete-event simulation, MRP and BOMs, OpenUSD export, Coding agents. https://pikulsomesh.github.io/michelin-kitchen-twin/
- Baby Senses Lab (World models; Live · paper on arXiv): AI world models train on adult-quality data from day one. Infants start with blurry, muffled input and still learn fast. What does that staging buy a model? One world model per sense (vision, hearing, touch, body position), each fed through an age-tuned filter and grown as it trains, then fused. The public site lets parents see and hear like a baby of any age; researchers get the findings, papers and code. Stack: PyTorch, World models, Network growth, Multisensory fusion. https://pikulsomesh.github.io/developmental-world-models/
- LabTrends (On-device AI; v1.1 released): A family's lab results sit in PDFs and paper scans from different clinics, and seeing a trend usually means handing health data to someone's cloud. An Android app that reads reports with on-device OCR, parses biomarkers with rules backed by a small local language model, and has a person confirm every value before it is saved. The release build has no internet permission at all. Stack: React Native + Expo, Local LLM (llama.rn), On-device OCR, Encrypted SQLite backups. https://github.com/pikulsomesh/LabTrends
- Academic Matchmaker (In-browser AI; In progress): Prospective PhD students choose advisors from rankings and cold emails rather than research fit. Drop in a CV or paper and a small language model running in the browser on WebGPU extracts research interests; embeddings then rank faculty across the top 100 universities. Nothing leaves the device. A scheduled pipeline is rebuilding the faculty index from open scholarly data. Stack: Transformers.js, WebGPU, Small LLM (ONNX), Embeddings search, React + Vite. https://github.com/pikulsomesh/academic-matchmaker
- Digital Twin History (Physical AI; Live): “Digital twin” means something different in every meeting. A shared, cited history gives teams a common vocabulary. An open dataset of milestones from andon lights and Apollo's simulators to AI world models and agentic twins, with a walkable 3D factory shown across six eras and research trends from OpenAlex. MIT licensed for courses and talks. Stack: Open dataset, three.js, OpenAlex, Vite. https://pikulsomesh.github.io/digital-twin-history/
- India Iceberg Index (AI and work; Technical paper): Most AI-and-jobs estimates count tech jobs. The larger exposure sits in everyday tasks across the whole economy. Adapts the Iceberg Index method to India: generative-AI exposure scores mapped to national occupation codes and weighted by 2023–24 labor survey data, district by district, with an interactive dashboard and a technical paper. Stack: Python, Streamlit, pydeck maps, Labor survey microdata. https://github.com/pikulsomesh/india-iceberg-index

## Playbook: how I think about data and AI at scale

The goal is not to turn a company into an AI company. It is to make data and AI a multiplier for the company it already wants to become.

### Ten beliefs

1. Start from the business's core learning problem. Every business has one quantity whose improvement compounds: yield, forecast accuracy, cycle time, first-pass quality. AI earns its budget by moving that number.
2. Data is an enterprise asset, not an IT by-product. Every critical domain needs a named owner, measurable quality, discoverability and accountable stewardship.
3. Context is the moat; models are a commodity. Anyone can rent a frontier model. The scarce asset is trusted, permissioned, versioned context an agent can act on.
4. The platform makes the second team faster than the first. Any capable group can ship one solution. A platform justifies itself when the fifth team ships in a fraction of the first team's effort.
5. Autonomy is earned per workflow. It is never a setting you switch on. The tier is set by how reversible an action is and what a wrong one costs.
6. Govern by design, so the safe path is the fast path. Identity, guardrails, policy and logging live in the platform, not in a committee at the end.
7. Evaluation is the product, not the QA step. The difference between a demo and a capability is that someone can tell you, on demand, whether it still works.
8. Every answer has a token bill. Most of it is avoidable. The harness matters more than the horsepower.
9. Central standards, federated delivery. Do once, centrally, what must be identical. Leave with the domains what needs proximity. Write the line down.
10. Measure decisions changed and value created. Not models built, pilots run or people trained. If Finance would not sign the number, it is not a result.

### 01. Strategy & value

Enterprises rarely need a parallel AI organization sitting beside the business. They need a small capability that makes every existing team measurably faster at what it already does. The test for any initiative: does it make an existing team's job easier, or does it add one more layer to manage?

#### The flywheel worth starting

- Trusted data: Owned domains with measured quality.
- Reusable data products and context: Defined once, used by every team.
- Shared AI platform: Gateway, evaluation, agents and paved paths.
- Better employee and customer experiences: Answers inside the tools people already use.
- Faster decisions and innovation: Cycle time, quality and cost move.
- More value, learning and adoption: Which feeds richer data back into the loop.


#### How I choose what goes first

A portfolio is a sequencing problem, not a wish list. The first capabilities set precedent, so they need to be the ones most likely to succeed and most likely to build the shared foundations everything else depends on. I score candidates on four filters.

- High volume: Enough repetitions a year that a small per-transaction gain compounds into something worth the engineering.
- Document-bound: The work is reading, extracting and deciding from text and records, which is where current models are strongest.
- Rules exist: There is a policy, playbook or standard to point to, so correctness can be checked rather than debated.
- Reversible: A wrong output is caught and corrected cheaply. Irreversible processes wait until the platform has a track record.

Alongside those near-term wins I always hold one bet on the core learning problem: a model inside the physical or scientific loop that removes cycles altogether. That is where the largest value usually sits.


#### The value case: what counts and what does not

Counts as value | Does not count
Cost per transaction before and after, with Finance agreeing the baseline | Hours saved multiplied by a loaded rate, presented as cash
Cycle time measured end to end, not just for the automated step | Headcount reductions not agreed with the leader who owns that headcount
Straight-through processing and exception rates, trended | Revenue attributed to a productivity tool
Capacity redeployed, named by team and role | Pilot results extrapolated to enterprise scale without a scaled measurement

One inflated benefit claim that fails an audit costs more credibility than three honest quarters earn. A smaller verified number is worth more than a larger arguable one.

### 02. Data foundation

Most AI disappointment traces back to data, not models. So no model work starts until the data it depends on is owned, defined and measured.

#### Ownership with names attached

- Owner: A business leader accountable for the domain's data and for hitting its quality targets.
- Steward: Owns definitions, business rules and the glossary for the domain.
- Custodian: Owns the pipelines, access controls and operational health of the data.


#### One pipeline, three layers of trust

- Sources: ERP, MES, CRM, PLM, historians, documents and sensors.
- Bronze: Raw ingest, immutable and replayable.
- Silver: Cleansed and conformed against the quality framework.
- Gold: Curated data products with owners and contracts.
- Catalog & lineage: Meaning is looked up, not inferred, from source column to decision.
- Agents & decisions: Analytics, models and agents consume Gold through the context layer.


#### Quality you can see

Dimension | The question it answers
Completeness | Are the required fields and records present?
Conformance | Does the data follow standards, formats, units and plausible ranges?
Consistency | Does the same business object mean the same thing in every system?
Accuracy & integrity | Do values reflect physical reality, and do relationships hold?
Timeliness & alignment | Is it fresh enough for the decision, and aligned in time across sensors and systems?

I track coverage in two directions: whether a standard exists for a domain, and whether it is actually in use at every site and system. "We have a standard" and "the standard is used everywhere" are different claims, and federation succeeds or fails on the second.

For a public account of this kind of journey, MIT CISR's case study follows how Caterpillar built a single, trusted data source and the adoption behind it. Wixom, Rodriguez, Piccoli and Beath, “Caterpillar's Digital Data Journey,” MIT CISR Working Paper No. 467 (2025): https://cisr.mit.edu/publication/MIT_CISRwp467_CaterpillarDataJourney_WixomRodriguezPiccoliBeath


#### No model before the data is ready

Every use case earns a data readiness score, technical and business, before development starts.

Technical readiness | Business readiness
Quality measured on the five dimensions | Every term the use case depends on is defined, owned and approved
Named owner, steward and custodian | The process is documented and mapped to its data
Column-level lineage from source to decision | The decision is mapped: who makes it today and what will change
Every Gold metric has a definition, unit, logic, valid range and owner | A named business owner and a measured baseline exist
Access rights and retention are clear | Legal basis, training and procedure updates are planned

Data quality is also an economics lever. Once meaning is looked up rather than inferred, every downstream model call spends fewer tokens working out what the data means.

### 03. Context & knowledge

The context layer is where a company's advantage actually lives. Models change every few months; decades of operating records, designs, procedures and expert know-how do not.
- A semantic layer: Business definitions fixed once, so "yield", "on-time" or "active customer" mean one thing to every person and every agent.
- Retrieval beyond vectors: Vector, graph and structured retrieval together. Many enterprise questions are relational, and graphs are the natural shape for lineage, networks and dependencies.
- Entitlements inherited from source: An agent can never surface data the requesting person could not open directly. Permissions travel with the data.
- Lineage and provenance: Every answer traces to the record that produced it, which is also how AI-assisted work earns a defensible audit trail.


#### Three levels of return

- Level 1 · Productivity: Specifications, procedures, design rules and quality records become discoverable and reusable.
- Level 2 · Innovation speed: New projects start from approved context, data products and components instead of rebuilding them.
- Level 3 · New products: Trusted context can eventually power customer-facing services. A strategic option, validated before it is committed.

Tacit knowledge deserves its own program. In plants and labs the most valuable know-how lives in experienced people. Capturing it as structured guidance, with their names on it, both protects the company and gives those experts the recognition they rarely get.

### 04. AI platform

Seven layers, each with one owner and one reason to exist. A layer belongs in the center only if doing it once, identically, is clearly better than doing it many times in context.
- L7 · Domain solutions: Built by domain teams on the paved path. Use-case selection, workflow redesign and domain evaluation criteria stay close to the work. Owner: Federated
- L6 · Golden paths: Scaffolds, SDKs, reference apps, release gates and templates for each authority tier. This is the product the platform team actually sells. Owner: Central
- L5 · Evaluation & observability: Golden datasets, regression gates, tracing, drift watch and continuous production sampling. Owner: Central, non-negotiable
- L4 · Agent runtime & orchestration: Tool registry, planning and memory, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, rollback and a tested kill switch. Owner: Central
- L3 · Model gateway: One path to every model: routing and fallback, caching, policy and PII filters, cost attribution per team. Owner: Central, mandatory
- L2 · Context: Semantic layer, vector, graph and structured retrieval, inherited entitlements, lineage. The moat. Owner: Central standards, domain-curated
- L1 · Data estate: Operational, engineering, commercial and enterprise data, delivered as governed data products. Owner: Domains, contracted to the platform
- Model lifecycle: Training, registry, locked production versions and drift monitoring tied to change control.
- Identity, audit & security: Who did what and when, keys, sensitive-data discovery and posture, applied the same way at every layer.

Governance spans every layer rather than sitting as a gate at the end. Cybersecurity, enterprise architecture, legal and finance are partners in the design, not reviewers of the result.

- Systems of record stay put: Operational, quality, planning and finance systems remain the record. AI reads from them and writes back only through approved workflows.
- Portable by choice: Open table formats, standard model packaging, OpenTelemetry traces and MCP tools keep each layer movable between clouds and data platforms.
- Accelerated where it pays: GPU-accelerated simulation and optimization for digital twins, routing and scheduling, used where the speed-up changes a decision rather than everywhere.


#### The gateway is the control point

- Control: Policy enforcement, PII and trade-secret filters, logging, data-residency routing and per-request identity. One place to change a rule and one place to prove it was applied.
- Economics: Cost attributed to the requesting team on every call, routing by task class, semantic caching and budget alerts. Finance sees a real bill by domain.
- Optionality: Provider abstraction, so a workload can move between model vendors or clouds as prices and terms change. Negotiating leverage becomes a design property.

Retrofitting a gateway after eighteen months of direct model calls is a year of painful work. A gateway that only routes, logs and attributes cost is worth more in month two than a complete platform in month nine, because it starts producing the usage data that tells you what to build next.


#### The golden path, end to end

- Intake · 1 week: A one-page business case: the workflow, the decision changed, the baseline, the named owner, the authority tier and the data. No production owner, no start.
- Scaffold · day one: A repository that already works, with gateway auth, approved retrieval, tracing, an evaluation stub and CI. The first commit is domain logic.
- Evaluate · continuous: No golden dataset, no promotion. Domains write the criteria; the platform runs the harness and regression gates on every change.
- Review · 3 days: One parallel review of security, privacy, responsible AI and architecture against a published checklist scaled to the tier.
- Deploy: Production means operated: a named owner, on-call, dashboards for quality, latency and cost, and a documented rollback.
- Measure · 30/90/180 days: The intake baseline is re-measured with Finance. Capabilities that miss their threshold are fixed or retired.

Step a builder faces | Without a paved path | On the golden path
Get model access | Open a vendor account, wait on legal, manage keys locally | One gateway credential, already reviewed
Reach trustworthy data | Find a source, negotiate access, re-implement permissions | Registered context sources with entitlements and lineage
Know if it works | Spot-check by hand and argue in a meeting | Golden dataset, scored runs, regression gate
Pass review | Four sequential queues and unclear standards | One parallel, tier-scaled review
Run it | Whoever built it, until they change roles | Named owner, on-call, dashboards, rollback
Prove value | A slide asserting hours saved | A baseline re-measured with Finance

The commitment I publish: intake decisions in five working days, a scaffold the day a use case is approved, combined review in three days for lower tiers. A central function that is slow and mandatory is worse than none, so if we miss, domains get a documented exception path.


#### Physical AI and digital twins

For operations-heavy businesses the platform extends into simulation. A physics-grounded digital twin of a plant, line or fleet becomes a place to test schedules, layouts and maintenance strategies before touching the real world, and a conversational layer lets planners query it in plain language. Physics stays in the loop: thermal limits, capacity constraints and degradation curves bound what a model may say, and hybrid physics-ML beats either alone when failure data is thin.

The cost of a first twin has also collapsed. It no longer has to start as a CAD-first project: existing video, a world model and open standards can stand up a usable facility twin in days, with the sensor layer designed and priced before anything is installed. Keeping OpenUSD as the only contract between capture, data and rendering means each layer can be swapped without rebuilding the rest.

As a worked example, I built a twin of a representative food bank from a public news video in seven days, with the data layer on AWS, rendering in NVIDIA Omniverse, and the cloud architecture and full cost published alongside the code. Mohapatra, “From Video to Digital Twin: Accelerating Spatial Twins with World Models and NVIDIA Omniverse” (2026): paper, code and live twin: https://github.com/pikulsomesh/foodbank-spatial-twin

### 05. Agentic systems

Autonomy is not a property of the technology. It is a permission granted per workflow, set by two questions: how reversible is the action, and how expensive is a wrong one?
- T1 · Assist: Reversible · low cost of error May: Retrieve, summarize, draft and explain. Output goes to a person who decides what to do with it. Control: The human is the actor. The agent never writes anywhere. Evidence to launch: Golden dataset, citation to source on every claim, light security review, usage telemetry.
- T2 · Propose: Reversible · moderate cost May: Prepare a complete action, such as a plan change, a case response or a document, and stage it for approval. Control: Explicit human approval before anything commits, logged with the reasoning shown. Evidence to launch: Everything in T1, plus approval and override rates and a review of what humans corrected.
- T3 · Act within bounds: Reversible · high volume May: Execute inside declared limits on value, scope and time. Escalate anything outside them. Control: Bounds enforced in the runtime, not the prompt. Kill switch and one-step rollback are mandatory. Evidence to launch: Everything in T2, plus shadow mode until agreement with humans clears a threshold, a full audit trail and sampled human review.
- T4 · Operate: Hard to reverse · high consequence May: Own a recurring process end to end and report by exception. Control: A named executive is accountable. Dual control on irreversible steps. Formal change management. Evidence to launch: Sustained T3 performance, a documented failure-mode analysis, and sign-off from the business owner, legal and cybersecurity.


#### The rules that make tiers real

- The tier is declared at intake and enforced by the runtime, not asserted in a design document.
- Tiers are earned, not assigned. Nothing launches above T2, and promotion requires evidence from live operation.
- Every agent has one named human owner who is accountable for its behavior and reachable when it misbehaves.
- Anything touching regulatory submissions, safety, product release or contractual commitments stays at T2 by default, however good the model gets.
- The kill switch is tested. An untested rollback is not a rollback.


#### Four patterns worth standardizing

- Grounded answer: Retrieve, ground, answer, cite. The workhorse. Measure retrieval quality, not just the answer.
- Structured extraction: Document to schema with confidence scores and a human queue for low-confidence fields. The highest near-term return in most enterprises.
- Tool-using workflow: Plan, call registered tools, check results, escalate. Tools are registered and permissioned centrally, never ad hoc.
- Monitor and escalate: Watch a stream, detect a condition, raise a case with the evidence attached.

A common mistake: building a multi-agent architecture because it is interesting. Most enterprise problems are one well-grounded model with good retrieval and a clean tool interface. Multi-agent designs multiply failure modes, cost and debugging effort, and should be used only where a single agent has demonstrably failed.

### 06. Governance, risk & responsible AI

Speed and control only conflict when governance is a committee. When it is written standards plus automated enforcement, both come from the same place.

#### What "production-ready" means, written down

Requirement | The bar | How it is enforced
Validation | A golden dataset with domain-written criteria, scored above an agreed threshold, with a regression gate on every model, prompt or retrieval change | Automated in CI; a failing gate blocks promotion
Traceability | Every output traceable to the sources and tool calls that produced it, retained as long as legal requires | Tracing on by default; absence fails the gate
Monitoring | Live quality, latency, cost, usage and escalation dashboards with alert owners | Provisioned by the platform at deploy
Ownership | A named technical owner, a named business owner, an on-call path and a tested rollback | Recorded in the service registry; no owner, no production
Risk management | Declared tier, runtime-enforced bounds, documented failure modes, a review cadence matched to the tier | Enforced by the runtime, reviewed at tier depth
Entitlements | The system never surfaces data the user could not access directly | Inherited from source at the context layer


#### Risk-tier every model, not just every agent

A meeting summarizer and a model that sets a process parameter, prices a contract or informs a regulatory filing do not deserve the same review. Higher tiers get locked model versions, formal change control, independent validation by people outside the build line, and drift monitoring with management-of-change when the process shifts. Lower tiers get a light, fast path. Proportion is what lets the organization move quickly where it is safe.


#### Anchored in recognized frameworks

Framework | How I use it
NIST AI RMF and its Generative AI Profile | The organizing structure: govern, map, measure, manage
ISO/IEC 42001 | The target AI management system, with certification readiness as an option where customers need evidence
ISO/IEC 23894 | The AI risk-assessment method
EU AI Act | Applied wherever operations reach the EU; most industrial uses are not high-risk, but HR and employment uses can be
OWASP LLM and agentic guidance, MITRE ATLAS | Threat taxonomy for red-teaming
NIST CSF 2.0, SP 800-53, IEC 62443 | Cyber and OT controls owned by security, with AI controls mapped onto them

The frameworks converge on four things: risk-based classification, transparency, meaningful human oversight and accountability. Every higher-tier review also asks three ethical questions: how serious could the harm be, who is most vulnerable, and who holds responsibility?


#### A short policy stack and a few clear forums

- Policy stack: AI policy and principles; acceptable use; risk classification; data for AI; model and agent lifecycle; third-party AI; AI incident response.
- Steering committee · quarterly: Strategy, risk appetite, funding and the highest-tier approvals, with internal audit observing.
- Governance council · bi-weekly: Lower-tier approvals, policy, exceptions and incidents, with security, legal, privacy and data governance.
- Data council and site champions · monthly: Standards, glossary, quality targets and data contracts; adoption, feedback and intake from the front line.


#### Risks I treat as first-class

- Intellectual property and trade secrets: contractual and technical guarantees that no vendor trains on company data, and classification-aware routing so the most sensitive material reaches only approved deployments.
- Regulatory and claims exposure: anything that could become a submission or a public claim stays human-approved with full traceability, indefinitely.
- Data residency and cross-border transfer: the gateway routes by data classification and jurisdiction, because asking each team to get it right is not a control.
- Entitlement leakage: zero tolerance, measured and reported.

### 07. Economics of AI

Enterprise AI programs rarely fail on capability. They stall when unit economics turn out to be indefensible at scale: a per-query cost that was invisible for forty pilot users becomes a line item someone has to defend for four thousand.

#### Where the money actually goes

- Context bloat: Stuffing everything retrievable into the window because it is easier than retrieving well. Usually the largest avoidable line.
- Over-powered routing: Sending classification and extraction to a frontier model because it was the scaffold default.
- Retry and loop waste: Agents that re-plan on ambiguity instead of escalating. Cost grows non-linearly.
- No caching: The same questions answered from scratch hundreds of times a day.


#### The optimization ladder

Move | What changes | Cost to implement
Retrieval discipline | Rank and trim context to what the task needs; often better accuracy too | Low
Task-class routing | Small models for classification and extraction, frontier models only for open reasoning | Low once the gateway exists
Semantic caching | Near-duplicate questions served from cache with freshness rules | Moderate
Batch versus interactive | Anything not waiting on a person moves to scheduled batch | Low
Distillation | A small model trained on a large one's traces for a narrow, stable, high-volume task | High; justified only at real volume

The harness matters more than the horsepower. A cheap model that starts with company context, the right skill pack and clean tools routinely beats an expensive model that has to research what the company is on every call.


#### What I report every month

- Cost per outcome by capability, trended: the headline number
- Spend by domain, attributed at the gateway and reconciled with Finance
- Cache hit rate, and the spend it avoided
- Routing mix by model class, with drift flagged
- Idle capability spend: what we pay for things nobody uses


#### Buy, partner or build

These decisions set cost structure, timelines and lock-in for years, so I run every one through the same short rubric. Answer the questions for a capability you are weighing.

- Buy: Clear market solutions exist and the capability is not a differentiator. Require modular, interoperable products on open standards, and an exit plan before signing. Typically: Workplace assistants, enterprise search, data catalogs, cloud security posture, managed model hosting.
- Partner: Share risk with front-runners on work that is not a product yet, or that matters but cannot yet be run in-house. We specify the architecture and own the result; the partner accelerates it. Typically: Physics-grounded digital twins, vision inspection at the line, integration with operational-technology data.
- Build selectively: Intersects core value creation and creates an advantage competitors cannot buy. Owned by employees, whoever writes the first version, and built on the shared platform. Typically: Process, yield and quality models, the business glossary and process maps, agents that act on proprietary data.

Partners accelerate work we have specified; they never define the architecture. Anything load-bearing, such as the gateway, the evaluation harness and the context layer, is owned by employees, whoever writes the first version. Every vendor faces three tests: can we leave within two quarters, does the contract prohibit training on our data, and does using it deepen our own team's capability or replace it?

- Composable: Modular parts that each do one thing well and connect through clean interfaces: APIs, MCP, OpenTelemetry, open table formats, SQL.
- Compostable: Every part replaceable without a redesign. The model chosen today will not be the one in production in eighteen months, so each decision is recorded with its exit plan.


#### Open-source alternatives, layer by layer

Layer | Open-source options | When I would consider them
Model hosting | vLLM, SGLang or TGI serving open-weight models | Data that must stay inside a controlled boundary; high, steady volume
Model gateway | LiteLLM | Routing across several providers with unified budgets
Agent runtime | LangGraph, Strands Agents, CrewAI; Temporal for durable execution | Edge or on-premises deployment near operations
Tool protocol | Self-hosted MCP servers | Always: it is the portable, open standard
Guardrails | NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, Llama Guard, Presidio for PII | Self-hosted models and custom domain rules
Observability | Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, OpenLLMetry, Grafana | Multi-cloud estates or an existing standard
Evaluation | Ragas, DeepEval, promptfoo | Evaluations that run in CI on every change
ML lifecycle | MLflow, Kubeflow, Feast; Evidently for drift | Models at the edge or across clouds
Context and catalog | DataHub, OpenMetadata | Budget limits and strong in-house engineering
Knowledge and search | OpenSearch-based retrieval, Vespa | Cost at scale or sovereign deployment
Data quality | Great Expectations, Soda Core, dbt tests | Almost always viable
Tables and compute | Apache Iceberg, Trino, Spark, DuckDB | Open format by default
Digital twins | OpenUSD, physics-ML libraries | OpenUSD as the interchange format

Open source is free to download, not free to run. Budget for patching, security review, support and license checks, since some open models carry use restrictions, and screen model provenance against the business's own supply-chain and customer requirements.

### 08. Organization & talent

The org chart is a leverage question, not a staffing question. A deliberately small central core owns what must be done once; embedded practitioners sit with the business; an independent function validates the highest-risk models.
- Embedded pods: Close to the decision. Data scientists and AI engineers sit with operations, supply chain, R&D, commercial and finance, with a business owner setting priorities and measuring value.
- Central platform & methods: Built once, used everywhere: platform engineering, evaluation and operations, architecture and governance.
- Independent validation: A small model-risk function that validates the highest-tier models and reports outside the build line, so the organization never grades its own work.


#### Who decides what

Role | Decides
Business domains | Which use cases are worth doing, what good output looks like, whether to accept the residual risk of a tier, when a capability stops being worth operating
Data & AI leadership | Architecture and the paved path, the production bar and release gates, model routing and cost controls, what is built centrally versus federated
Executive sponsor | Ambition and risk appetite, funding, cross-business trade-offs, the highest-tier authorizations
Security, legal, risk | Enterprise controls, the operational-technology boundary, regulatory interpretation


#### What each side owes the other

The core owes the domains | The domains owe the core
An intake decision in 5 days | A named production owner
A working scaffold the same day | An agreed baseline
Review in 3 days | Evaluation criteria for their workflow
Published standards, working examples and a person who answers | Use of the paved path, or a documented exception


#### Talent: the part only a leader can do

- Hire deliberately mixed profiles: Statisticians and forecasters, optimization specialists, ML and GenAI engineers who ship, and domain engineers who want to model.
- Grow on a real technical ladder: Principal and distinguished tracks that pay as well as management, so the best scientists keep doing science.
- Rotate for domain fluency: Embedded practitioners spend two or three quarters in a domain, then return to the core with what they learned. Patterns that work become part of the paved path.
- Four competency tracks: Platform engineering, applied AI engineering, AI product management, and evaluation and operations, each with levelled expectations and portfolio-based promotion.
- One hiring bar: Structured hiring and performance management across every location, the same process I built from zero at a startup and run today across two countries.
- Literacy beyond the team: Analysts, engineers and leaders across the business learn to frame a decision, read a forecast interval and question a model.

### 09. Change & adoption

Adoption is earned, not mandated. If someone can get an answer faster by going around the platform, they will, and they should. That is a defect report about the platform.
- Capacity, not cuts: The goal is fewer repetitive tasks, faster decisions and more room for engineering, customer and creative work. Where workforce change is genuinely needed, the answer is transparency, reskilling and redeployment, not a promise that technology never affects jobs.
- Teams move up the stack: Existing BI and analytics teams are developed, not displaced. They move from one-off reports to building the reusable data products and agentic tools everyone else uses.
- Treat internal users as customers: Design for the person doing the work, not the reporting layer. A tool that costs a frontline user time will be abandoned by week three, whatever the mandate says.
- Earn trust before asking for it: Start with grounded, cited assistance. Never ask an expert to trust a model whose failure modes you cannot explain. Experts forgive a model that is uncertain and never forgive one that is confidently wrong.
- A literacy ladder open to everyone: AI fluency is a company-wide ladder anyone can climb, not a perk for a technical elite.
- Listening before pitching: Every program starts with listening on the floor, in the lab and with the field teams. The AI lead in the room is not the domain expert, and should not act like one.


#### One front door

Getting an answer today often means knowing which system holds the data, which analyst owns it, whether a dashboard exists and whom to ask if it does not. The end state is one governed front door, inside each person's existing permissions, that composes an answer or a live view from approved data products rather than a one-off chat reply. It is also the single best lever on cost, because every call starts warm with the right context.

### 10. How a program matures

Data and AI programs that last move through recognizable stages, and each stage has a different job: understand, decide, ship, prove, widen and industrialize. Skipping a stage is how most programs stall. The early work is weighted toward listening and toward domain knowledge: architecture can be proposed quickly, but understanding how the business actually runs cannot.
- Stage 1 · Baseline what exists: Most programs begin with more AI activity than anyone has counted. The first job is an honest inventory of every initiative, with its cost, its owner and whether it is really in production, alongside an understanding of how the work actually runs on the floor, in the lab and in the field. Security, legal, architecture and finance are engaged here so they shape the standards rather than review them. Deliverable: A written baseline and a shortlist of lighthouse use cases with named owners.
- Stage 2 · Decide and publish: Platform architecture agreed. The production-ready definition and authority tiers drafted with security, legal and compliance, then published. Gateway build started. Team design confirmed. Two lighthouse use cases selected, with baselines agreed in writing with Finance. Deliverable: Published standards, an agreed roadmap, a funded plan, two use cases in build.
- Stage 3 · Ship something real: Gateway live with routing, logging and cost attribution, plus a migration plan for existing direct model use. Golden path v1. The first lighthouse in production with a named owner, dashboards and a measured baseline. The first monthly value and cost report. Deliverable: A working platform with one real capability on it.
- Stage 4 · Prove the path: Second lighthouse in production. All new AI work uses the gateway. Embedded practitioners deployed. Review service levels published and reported. Competency model released. First value re-measurement against the agreed baselines.
- Stage 5 · Widen: Every priority area has at least one production capability. Cost-per-outcome trends reported. The first rotation completes and its lessons join the paved path. Vendor strategy formalized under the two-quarter exit test.
- Stage 6 · Industrialize: Reuse rate becomes a reported metric. The first capabilities are retired for missing their value threshold, a sign of health. The next roadmap is built with domain leaders, not for them.


#### What a maturing program should be able to show

- A platform every team uses because it is the fastest route, with a pilot-to-production rate anyone can state as a number.
- A benefits register agreed with Finance, with baselines captured before launch and figures that hold up line by line.
- A production bar enforced in the release gate, zero entitlement violations, and security, legal and compliance calling themselves co-authors.
- A reported, rising reuse rate and a retired-capabilities list that is not empty.
- A lean team on a published competency model, with internal candidates filling senior roles.

### 11. The scorecard

Model count, pilot count and people trained are activity metrics. They tell a leadership team nothing about whether the investment was worth making. These are the measures a program should be held to.
Dimension | Metric | How the baseline is set
Business value | Verified annualized benefit by capability: cost, cycle time, capacity released | Measured before launch, agreed with Finance, re-measured at 30, 90 and 180 days
Speed | Cycle time in the targeted process; experiments or iterations avoided | Prior-period actuals from the system of record
Adoption | Weekly active users by function; repeat use at month six | Zero at launch; targets set per capability
Pilot to production | Share of initiated use cases reaching production with a named owner | The initial inventory
Reuse | Share of new solutions built on the paved path | Zero at launch
Unit economics | Cost per resolved task, by capability, monthly | First month of gateway telemetry
Reliability | Uptime, latency and quality against the golden dataset | Set at production entry
Data quality | Five-dimension scores and coverage by domain and site | First data readiness assessment
Risk | Review findings; entitlement violations | Zero tolerance for entitlement violations
Capability | Practitioners at each competency level; internal fill rate | Team baseline at program start

Reporting is short enough to be read: one page monthly on value, cost, adoption, reliability and risk; a quarterly portfolio review of what is being promoted and what is being retired.

The uncomfortable metric: capabilities retired for missing their value threshold. If that number is zero after a year, either the thresholds are not real or nobody is checking. I report it deliberately.

### 12. What I avoid

These are the commitments that are easy to make at the start of a program and hard to keep in month eight, when something is behind and a shortcut is available.
- Build a shadow delivery organization: A central team that competes with domain teams ends up owning a portfolio it cannot operate. The platform's product is the paved path.
- Start a pilot without a production owner: The pilot graveyard is filled with pilots nobody was ever going to run. Saying no early is worth more than the pilot.
- Grant autonomy before evaluation exists: No agent acts without a golden dataset, a measured threshold, a tested rollback and a named owner.
- Accept lock-in for short-term speed: If we cannot leave within two quarters, it is a strategy commitment, not a tool choice, and it goes to the executive sponsor.
- Chase a model zoo: Supporting every new model and framework is a maintenance tax. A small approved set, reviewed on a schedule.
- Overstate the value: No hours-times-rate arithmetic presented as cash and no pilot results extrapolated to the enterprise.
- Centralize domain judgment: What counts as a good answer in a domain is the domain's call. The moment the center defines it, the standards stop being trusted.
- Hire ahead of the operating model: Twenty people without a paved path produce twenty bespoke solutions. Run light, then hire into a structure that makes each person more effective.

## Build notes and essays

### Food Bank Spatial Twin

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/foodbank-spatial-twin/ · 2026-10-28

A working digital twin of a representative Texas food bank, built from a public news video in seven days for about $1.54 of compute. No CAD drawings, no laser scans, no site visit. Five parts, from why to the full pipeline and the paper.

Digital twins help warehouses plan, schedule and catch failures early, but most of them start from CAD drawings or laser scans. That puts them out of reach for the organizations that could use one and can least afford one, like a regional food bank running a warehouse-scale cold chain on a non-profit budget.

This build asks a narrow question: is a publicly available video tour enough to start a useful twin? The answer turned out to be mostly yes. Frames from a local news tour went through a world model and a locally trained Gaussian-splat model to become 3D captures of four areas. A Blender script modeled the rest of the building. A serverless AWS backend serves operations data in the same coordinates, and the twin runs in a browser and in NVIDIA Omniverse. OpenUSD is the only contract between the steps.

The twin is a representative food bank inspired by that tour, not a model of any one site, and nobody at the food bank or the news station was involved. Every part of it is labeled as captured, designed, published, estimated or simulated. It is a personal project, done in personal time, because food security matters and because this is the cheapest way I know to show what the current tools can do.

 How to read the series

Each part stands on its own and links to the exact code it describes. Part 1 is the why. Parts 2 to 4 each take one layer: the captures, the building, and the cloud. Part 5 puts the whole pipeline together with the numbers and the paper.

### Academic Matchmaker

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/academic-matchmaker/ · 2026-10-28

How I built a private, in-browser search that matches a CV against 181,568 researchers at the world's top 200 universities. Covers fitting the index into a static site, semantic matching with a small model, and why concept tags had to come next.

Choosing a PhD or postdoc advisor is one of the biggest decisions in an academic career, and it is still done by hand. Students read faculty pages one university at a time, guess at fit from paper titles, and cold-email people whose research moved on years ago.

The Academic Matchmaker turns that into a search problem. You drop in a CV, a paper or a Google Scholar screenshot, and it ranks researchers across the top 200 universities by how closely their recent work matches yours. Two constraints shaped every decision:

- Nothing you upload leaves your device. Text extraction, the language model and the matching all run in the browser.
- No servers. The site is static files on GitHub Pages. The data is rebuilt by GitHub Actions and served from a Hugging Face dataset.

Those two constraints are what make this build interesting. Fitting 181,568 researchers into something a browser can search in a second or two took a series of storage and ranking decisions. They are worth writing down because the same moves apply to any retrieval system with a tight budget.

 The three parts

Part 1 covers the problem and the architecture. Part 2 is the data pipeline and storage: how 200 universities of OpenAlex data are ingested under a free API budget and squeezed from about 280 MB of vectors down to under 9 MB. Part 3 is matching: the small model in the browser, coarse-to-fine vector search, why pure semantic matching was not enough, and the concept tags and laureate test set that fixed it.

### Michelin Kitchen Twin

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/michelin-kitchen-twin/ · 2026-10-28

A browser-based digital twin of a three-Michelin-star kitchen running a full dinner service, modeled the way a factory is. Recipes are bills of materials, covers are the build plan, and a deterministic simulation drives a photoreal 3D kitchen and an operations dashboard.

I have always been fascinated by how great kitchens work. On a busy night, a tasting-menu restaurant makes hundreds of plates, each one to order, timed to the minute, and inspected before it leaves. That is high-mix, low-volume, just-in-time production with shared machines, skilled labor, perishable inventory and a customer who will not wait. It is the hardest case most factories face, and kitchens solve it every night without software.

So I built a twin of one, using the same vocabulary a plant would. The restaurant is the one with the most published detail about its kitchen, menu and recipes. Every record in the data cites a source or is marked as an estimate. Pick the number of covers, press play, and a deterministic simulation runs the night. Tickets fire, cooks move, ovens fill, stock drains and the bottleneck moves. The 3D kitchen, the dashboard and the Studio are all views of that one simulation.

 The five parts

Part 1 is why a kitchen is a good test of a digital twin. Part 2 is the data model: recipes as bills of materials and routings, and the MRP explosion. Part 3 is the discrete-event simulation, KPIs and the optimizer. Part 4 is the photoreal 3D kitchen and the Studio, in about half a megabyte. Part 5 is how five parallel AI agent threads built the first version in a day.

### Food Bank Spatial Twin, part 1: Why I built a food bank digital twin from a news video

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/foodbank-spatial-twin/why-a-food-bank-twin/ · 2026-10-28

Digital twins usually start from CAD drawings and laser scans, which most non-profits cannot pay for. I wanted to know whether a public video tour is enough to start one, and what that would cost.

A digital twin is a virtual copy of a site that stays in sync with it through data. In factories and warehouses, twins are used to plan layouts, watch equipment, and rehearse a change before anyone moves a rack. When they work, they pay for themselves.

The expensive part is almost never the dashboard. It is the geometry. A facility twin usually starts with CAD drawings, a laser-scanning crew, or a photogrammetry campaign, and then a specialist spends weeks importing all of it into a simulation tool. For an automotive plant that cost is a rounding error. For a regional food bank it is the whole reason a twin never happens.

 Why a food bank

A large food bank is a serious operation. It receives trucks at a dock, stores thousands of pallets in racking, runs freezers and coolers that cannot be allowed to drift, sorts donations with volunteer crews, and ships to hundreds of partner pantries. Many also run a client market and a community kitchen in the same building. That is a warehouse, a cold chain and a small food plant under one roof.

Those are exactly the problems twins are good at. Where is the inventory? Is the freezer holding temperature? Which dock is congested at 10 a.m. on a Monday? Where do the forklifts and the volunteers cross paths? The difference is the budget. Food banks run on donations and volunteer hours, so a six-figure scanning and modeling project is out of the question.

So the question I set myself was narrow and practical: is a publicly available video tour enough to start a useful twin, with no CAD drawings, no laser scans and no site visit? And if it is, how fast and how cheap can it be?

 What changed that made this worth trying

Three things moved in the last two years.

- World models and Gaussian splatting. A world model is an AI system that infers 3D structure from images. Given a few video frames, it can estimate where the camera was and how far away everything is in real metres. 3D Gaussian splatting turns posed images into a photorealistic 3D scene that renders in real time, even in a browser.
- OpenUSD can now hold splats. Universal Scene Description, the open 3D standard that came out of Pixar, added a native Gaussian-splat schema in its 26.03 release. A splat capture is no longer a viewer-specific file. It can sit in the same scene as racking, sensors and a forklift.
- Serverless cloud costs nothing at this scale. A backend that serves a twin's live data can be a few functions behind an API, and it bills only when someone calls it.

Put together, those three suggest a different order of work. Start from footage that already exists, get a first twin in days, and only spend real money on the parts that turn out to matter.

 The rules I set before writing any code

I gave myself seven days and three rules.

1. One contract between the steps. Everything upstream writes OpenUSD in metres, Y up, with the floor at zero. Everything downstream reads it. The browser, Blender and Omniverse are interchangeable renderers, not separate projects.
2. Label everything. Every part of the twin is tagged as captured from the video, designed for this project, taken from published figures, estimated, or simulated. A twin that hides which parts are real is worse than no twin.
3. Never pay twice. Every paid call has a budget cap, records its job id before waiting, and resumes instead of re-paying when it is run again.

The subject is a representative Texas food bank, inspired by a local news tour of one. It is not a replica of that building, and neither the food bank nor the station had any part in it.

 What came out of it

The pipeline runs in three steps, and each one gets its own part in this series.

- Video to 3D captures. Twenty frames went to a world model for camera poses and metric depth, and came back as about 747,000 splats across three areas, for 200 credits, which is 20 US cents. A Gaussian-splat trainer I wrote to run on a plain CPU then trained four areas from 49 to 72 frames each, at no credit cost, which made them hold up as the camera moves.
- The rest of the building in Blender. The video never shows the whole building, and asking the world model to imagine the unfilmed areas failed on the provider's side twice. So one headless Blender script models the full facility from the footprints in the operations data and publishes it in the same OpenUSD frame.
- Data on AWS, viewed anywhere. A serverless API on AWS serves cold-room telemetry, forklift positions and the operations layer in the same coordinates. The twin runs in a browser on GitHub Pages and renders in NVIDIA Omniverse on a rented GPU.

It went from first commit to a deployed backend in seven days. The build cost about $1.54 of compute: 20 cents of world-model credits and about $1.34 of GPU time for the Omniverse trials. The AWS backend has billed $0.00 so far. Putting real sensors on a facility floor is estimated at about $2,700 of hardware once and about $12 a month on AWS.

Not everything worked, and I will be specific about what did not. Generating views of unfilmed space failed. Omniverse rendered the Blender building beautifully but drew the splats as a blank grey frame. Those failures are as useful as the successes, because they show exactly where the tooling is today.

 What is next in the series

Part 2 goes into the first step in detail: how to get from a news video to a 3D world model, the frame selection and masking that make or break it, and the CPU splat trainer, with the code. After that come the Blender building, the AWS architecture, and the full pipeline with the paper.

The code, the docs and the live twin are all public. If you run a warehouse, a cold chain or a food bank and want to try this on your own footage, the repository is the place to start.

### Food Bank Spatial Twin, part 2: From a news video to a 3D world model

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/foodbank-spatial-twin/video-to-world-model/ · 2026-10-28

How twenty frames of a public video tour became metric 3D captures through a world model, and how a Gaussian-splat trainer running on a plain CPU made them photoreal, with the code for each step.

Part 1 was the why. This part is the first step of the pipeline: turning an 18-minute local news tour into 3D captures that sit in real metres. It is also the step where most of the judgment lives, because the video was shot for television, not for reconstruction.

 Start by reading the video like a surveyor

A world model needs overlapping views of one space, so the first job is to pick zones, not to process the whole tour. I sampled one frame every ten seconds and scored each stretch of the video for camera movement, people in shot, and surfaces that reconstruct badly.

 Zone  Verdict 
------
 Pallet-racking aisle  Picked first. The camera moves around a bay and down the aisle, and one stretch has no people at all 
 Volunteer sorting room  Picked. Clean shots, but the camera barely moves 
 Client market  Picked. Good shelves, people block the centre 
 Freezer and cooler doors  Skipped. Blank walls and fog 
 Community kitchen  Trained later. Stainless steel is hard for splats 

The racking aisle is also the zone that matters most for a warehouse twin: inventory locations, forklift paths and temperature zones all live there.

 Frames, and why the automatic picker failed

The script keeps the sharpest frame in each time bucket and crops off the broadcast graphics at the bottom of the screen.

The obvious way to pick eight inputs from forty is to split the clip into equal segments and take the sharpest frame in each. On interview footage that fails: sharpness rewards in-focus faces, so it picked six nearly identical shots of the two hosts. I chose the inputs by hand for viewpoint spread and fewest people, and masked the hosts out with boxes.

 The world model: poses and metric depth for 20 cents

The world model's pose task takes the frames and returns, for each one, where the camera was, a depth map in metres, and a confidence map. It costs 10 credits per image, and 1,000 credits is a dollar. Three zones from 20 frames came to 200 credits.

The depth passed a simple sanity check. The first racking beam lands about 0.4 m above the lens, which is what you would expect on a real beam about 1.9 m off the floor.

The fusion step is local and free. It unprojects every depth map, keeps the most confident sample per 1 cm voxel, and writes the result as Gaussians in both a browser format and OpenUSD.

Every paid stage writes its operation id to a state file before it waits, and sends an idempotency key derived from the request body, so a re-run resumes instead of paying again. The client also backs off on rate limits and gateway errors, honoring Retry-After:

A budget guard sits in front of every paid stage. If the estimate for a request is above --max-credits, the script refuses to submit it.

The step I most wanted, generating views of the space the camera never saw, failed twice on the provider's side with no detail. I stopped retrying until I knew whether failed jobs were billed. That is the open problem, and it is why Part 3 exists.

 Making it photoreal on a CPU

The fused captures look right from their source cameras and fall apart when you move. So the second route trains a real 3D Gaussian Splatting model per zone from 49 to 72 frames.

The standard trainers rasterize with CUDA kernels, and the machine that builds this repo has no GPU. So scripts/splattrain.py implements the same method in plain PyTorch tensor code: project each Gaussian to the image, composite front to back, and optimize color, shape and opacity against the frames. With sparse rasterization it runs at about one second per step at 480 pixels on four CPU cores.

The heart of it is compositing. Each pixel's color is a sum over the Gaussians that cover it, front to back, each weighted by its own opacity times the transmittance left by everything in front of it. On a GPU that is a loop per pixel. In tensor code it becomes one sorted list of (pixel, Gaussian) pairs and a segmented cumulative sum of log(1 − alpha), so transmittance for every pair comes out of one cumsum:

Pairs that would add less than 1/255 alpha are dropped before this step, and each Gaussian only touches pixels inside its visible extent. That is what keeps the work proportional to real coverage instead of image size times splat count.

Two details made the difference on news footage:

- Background plates. The hosts are in nearly every frame. Under their masks, the loss sees pixels warped in from frames up to 15 seconds away, where the hosts had moved on. Without that, the space behind them trains to haze.
- Visual-hull carving. Because the hosts walk with the camera, the space they occupy gets densified into grey columns of splats. Every 250 steps the trainer removes splats that land on a host mask in most of the frames that see them.

On a free cloud notebook GPU, the same stages run at full resolution with up to 1.5 million splats.

 The output contract

Both routes write the same thing: a splat file for the browser and an OpenUSD file in metres, Y up, with the floor at zero. Nothing downstream needs to know which route made a zone, which is the point.

Part 3: the video never shows the whole building, so how do you model the rest of it? The answer is one Blender script.

### Food Bank Spatial Twin, part 3: Modeling the rest of the building in Blender, from footprints

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/foodbank-spatial-twin/blender-facility-model/ · 2026-10-28

Splat captures only read well from where the camera stood. One headless Blender script models the whole food bank from the operations data and publishes it to the browser and Omniverse in the same OpenUSD frame.

The captures from Part 2 are real, but they are fragments. Each one looks right from its source cameras and breaks up anywhere else, and together they cover a small fraction of the building. The world model was supposed to fill the gaps, and that step failed. A twin that only exists where a news crew happened to walk is not a twin.

 Model the building from the data, not from the video

The fix was to stop asking the video for things it never showed. The operations data already describes the site: the footprint of each area, the cold rooms and their temperature probes, the docks, the racking rows. So the building is modeled from that data, by one script, with Blender running headless as a Python library.

The script builds the shell and dock doors with a trailer, a cut-away freezer and cooler racked inside, four rows of red selective racking with pallets, receiving and order staging, the volunteer sorting room with roller conveyors and scales, the client market, the community kitchen annex, painted lanes, signage and forklifts. The fit-out is inspired by what the video shows. The layout is designed, and labeled as designed.

Every area is a few lines of data-driven calls. The racking aisles, for example, are four rows placed in the same coordinates the telemetry uses:

Underneath, geometry is built from boxes whose hidden faces are skipped, and meshes are merged per area and material. That is why the browser model draws in about 150 calls instead of thousands.

 Same frame as everything else

The model is built in the same coordinate frame as the telemetry: metres, Y up, origin at the dock-door corner. That one decision is why everything lines up without manual fiddling.

 The temperature badges in the browser sit on the cold rooms, the forklift drives the route the telemetry describes, and the captured splats drop into their places on the floor plan.

 One scene, two outputs

From a single Blender scene the script writes:

- facility.glb for the browser, about 1.8 MB and about 150 draw calls, so it runs on a phone. One named node is the forklift the live data animates.
- facility.usdz for Omniverse and other OpenUSD tools, same frame, same names.
- Optionally a .blend to open on a desktop and a Cycles render of the overview.

Every texture is generated procedurally at build time, so the model needs no downloads and the whole thing rebuilds from the repo in minutes.

 Why scripted beats hand-modeled here

A hand-built model is a one-off. A scripted one is a function of the data. Change a footprint in the operations file, and the building, the browser view and the Omniverse stage all change with it on the next build. That is the same discipline a plant uses when the bill of materials drives the build, applied to a building.

Part 4: the cloud layer. How the data side runs on AWS for $0.00 so far, and what it took to get Omniverse rendering on a rented GPU.

### Food Bank Spatial Twin, part 4: The cloud layer, a digital twin backend on AWS for $0.00

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/foodbank-spatial-twin/aws-architecture/ · 2026-10-28

A serverless AWS backend serves telemetry and operations data in the twin's own coordinates, a real-sensor path is designed and priced, and Omniverse runs on EC2 GPUs that terminate themselves. What worked and every pitfall.

A twin is geometry plus data. Parts 2 and 3 built the geometry. This part is the data side and where it runs, with one design rule: everything bills only while it runs.

 The backend is three resources

The whole backend is one AWS SAM template:

 Resource  What it does 
------
 S3 bucket  Holds the twin's published assets and a copy of the site 
 HTTP API  GET /telemetry, GET /operations, GET /health, throttled to 5 requests a second 
 Lambda (Python, arm64, 128 MB)  Computes the current state of the building from the clock. Stateless, so there is no database 

/telemetry returns freezer, cooler and dry-storage temperature, humidity, door state and alarms, plus a forklift looping through the building. /operations returns inventory, flows, docks and the kitchen. Every position is in metres in the same frame as the OpenUSD scene, so a viewer can pin a badge to a cold room without a lookup table. Every payload says simulated: true.

Each cost decision is written into the template, next to the setting it controls:

No NAT gateway, no VPC, no provisioned capacity and no database means nothing bills while nobody is looking.

Measured after deployment: 1,000 sequential calls all succeeded, with a 67 ms median round trip. Cost Explorer showed $0.00 for the month, inside the free tier. Past the free tier, a viewer polling every five seconds around the clock is roughly 60 cents a month.

 The contract is the product

The simulator is deliberately thin. What matters is the JSON contract, because a real feed replaces the simulator without touching any renderer. The real-floor path is designed and priced: LoRaWAN and Bluetooth sensors into AWS IoT Core, a Lambda to normalize, DynamoDB for state. For one facility that is about $2,700 of hardware once and about $12 a month to run.

The same design maps onto Azure and Google Cloud, with two honest caveats. Azure IoT Hub has no LoRaWAN network server, so it needs a partner. Google Cloud IoT Core was retired in 2023. Both are designs only and have never been deployed.

All three diagrams are generated from one script into editable draw.io files, so they stay in step with each other.

 Security on the floor: read-only by design

A twin that connects to a facility is also a path into it, so the real-floor design treats the plant network the way industrial sites do. It follows the Purdue model's zones and conduits. Sensors and gateways sit on the floor. A small OT DMZ passes only outbound TLS, with no inbound ports. Every device has its own key or certificate. The cloud side ingests readings and sends no commands, so the twin is read-only. Existing refrigeration and dock controls stay in charge of their own alarms, and the only designed path back toward the floor is a signed, human-approved firmware update. The diagrams draw these trust boundaries as red dashed lines.

 Omniverse on a GPU that cannot outlive the job

Omniverse needs a GPU, and a GPU left running is the classic cloud bill surprise. So the render runs on a single EC2 instance launched for one job: no SSH key, no IAM role, inputs and outputs through presigned S3 URLs, a hard shutdown timer, and shutdown set to terminate. Two lines do most of the work. The user-data script starts with a hard cap, and the launch request says that a shutdown means termination, not a stopped instance that keeps its disk:

 Seven runs took about 94 instance-minutes and about $1.34.

It took seven runs because of these, in the order I hit them:

1. Driver too new. The current Deep Learning AMI's driver crashed Isaac Sim 5.1 a second after start, even on an empty scene. Plain Ubuntu with the 580 server driver worked.
2. Test with a cube first. A one-cube stage separates "the GPU stack is broken" from "my scene is broken". It took four runs to learn the scene was never the problem.
3. New accounts have zero GPU quota. Ask on day one. Approval took about an hour, plus 30 minutes to apply.
4. Budget 12 minutes to the first frame. Boot, a 4.5-minute container pull, and a 5-minute shader cache build. Render everything in one session.
5. Have a fallback instance type. On the last run there was no g6.xlarge capacity in the region. A g5.xlarge ran the same setup unchanged.
6. Splats rendered blank. Omniverse rendered the Blender building in RTX, but drew the splat captures as a grey frame. The browser shows the splats instead.

Part 5: the whole pipeline end to end, the full cost picture, and the paper.

### Food Bank Spatial Twin, part 5: The whole pipeline, what it cost, and the paper

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/foodbank-spatial-twin/pipeline-and-paper/ · 2026-10-28

The food bank twin end to end, from video to world model to Blender to AWS to Omniverse, with the full cost picture, what is real versus simulated, what failed, and the paper that documents it.

Four parts, four layers. This one puts them together, adds up the cost, and points to the paper that writes it all down properly.

 The pipeline on one page

OpenUSD is the only interface between the steps. That is what makes the renderer a deployment choice: the browser for anyone with a link, Omniverse when you need RTX and simulation, Blender on a laptop.

 What it cost

  Cost 
------
 This build: world model, local training, Blender, AWS, GPU trials  about $1.54 
 Capture to deployed twin for a full facility of about 135,000 sq ft  about $25 to $50 of cloud spend 
 Real sensors on the floor  about $2,700 once, about $12 a month 
 Omniverse on demand, 10 hours a week  about $124 a month 

These are directional, from public list prices and one individual AWS account. Enterprise discounts, quotas and policies will differ.

 What is real, and what is not

 Part  Kind 
------
 Racking aisle, sorting room, client market, community kitchen  Captured from the video, partial 
 Absolute scale  Estimated from the world model's metric depth 
 Building shell, cold rooms, staging, kitchen annex  Designed 
 Volumes, capacities, recipes, step times  Published figures or flagged estimates 
 Temperatures, doors, forklifts, inventory  Simulated, and every payload says so 

 What failed

Generating views of unfilmed space failed twice on the provider's side. Omniverse loaded the splat captures and drew them blank. Both are listed in the repo with what I tried. Filling in unseen space is the open step, and it is the one I expect the next round of world models to close.

 The paper

The build is written up as a paper: From Video to Digital Twin: Accelerating Spatial Twins with World Models and NVIDIA Omniverse. It covers the method, the provenance labels, the measurements, and the limits, with three supplementary movies. Read the PDF, or browse the LaTeX source and figures in the repository's paper/ folder.

 What I would tell someone starting one

- Start from footage you already have. It is enough to get a first twin and to find out which parts are worth real money.
- Pick the contract first. Metres, Y up, floor at zero, one scene format. Everything else becomes swappable.
- Label provenance from day one. It is what lets people trust the parts that are real.
- Make every paid step resumable and capped, and make cloud GPUs unable to outlive their job.

If you want the same approach applied to a very different operation, the Michelin Kitchen Twin series models a three-star kitchen the way a plant is modeled.

### Academic Matchmaker, part 1: A private research matchmaker that runs entirely in the browser

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/academic-matchmaker/private-research-matchmaker/ · 2026-10-28

Why I built an advisor search that matches a CV against 181,568 researchers without uploading anything, and the architecture that makes it possible on a static site with no servers.

Finding a PhD or postdoc advisor works roughly the way it did twenty years ago. You open a university's faculty page, read through a few hundred names, open the ones that sound close, skim their recent papers, and repeat for the next university. Twenty universities in, you have a spreadsheet, a headache, and no idea whether the best fit for your work was at the twenty-first.

The information to do better is public. OpenAlex indexes hundreds of millions of papers with author and institution links. ORCID records list people's current roles. University directories list emails. What is missing is a tool that puts it together and answers one question: whose recent research is closest to mine?

 Two constraints that shaped everything

I set two rules before writing code.

Your CV never leaves your device. A CV is personal. People upload drafts, unpublished work and contact details. A matching service that collects them is a liability for the person running it, and asking students to trust it is a big ask. So text extraction, the language model and the ranking all run in the visitor's browser.

No servers. The site is static files on GitHub Pages. The data is rebuilt by GitHub Actions on a schedule and published to a Hugging Face dataset, which serves it over a CDN. Nothing runs between those builds, so there is nothing to keep up and nothing to pay for.

Those two rules turn a standard retrieval problem into a constrained one. A typical setup would put the vectors in a database and run a query on a server. Here, the browser has to download whatever it searches, so every byte counts and the index has to be organized for partial loading.

 How a match happens

1. Read the upload. PDFs go through pdf.js. Screenshots of a Google Scholar or LinkedIn page go through Tesseract OCR. Saved HTML and text are read directly. You can also paste an ORCID iD or OpenAlex link, and the profile is built from public records instead.
2. Understand it. A small language model, Qwen2.5-0.5B quantized to 4 bits, runs on WebGPU (with a WebAssembly fallback) and extracts research interests as JSON. Chat messages go through the same model and refine the profile.
3. Embed it. The same sentence-embedding model that indexed the researchers, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, turns the profile into one 384-dimension vector.
4. Rank, coarse to fine. The browser scores 426 cluster centroids, downloads only the nearest clusters, and ranks the people in them.
5. Explain it. Each match shows the shared topics and the closest recent papers, so you can see why someone came up.

Two loading decisions matter for the first visit. The language model is a few hundred megabytes, so it loads only when someone types in the chat box. An uploaded CV skips it entirely and is matched with the embedding model alone. And the vectors load cluster by cluster, so a search touches a few percent of the index, not all of it.

 What it covers today

The build pipeline now indexes 181,568 researchers across the top 200 universities in the QS 2026 rankings, and 51,430 of them have an email that matches their name and their university's domain. The data refreshes monthly, with new papers and citations pulled from OpenAlex.

A fixed test set keeps the matching honest. It holds the 2026 Fields Medal and Nobel Prize winners. After every data refresh, the pipeline builds a profile for each of them from their public record (and from a saved CV where one exists), runs it through the same matcher the site uses, and checks the results. The last run passed 11 of 11. The site shows a "Prize test passing" badge only when that holds.

 Why this is worth writing up

The interesting part is not the interface. It is the series of decisions that made a 181,568-person index searchable on a phone without a server:

- splitting the pipeline into one job per university so it fits a free API budget and resumes when it hits the limit,
- storing search rows at about 100 bytes a person instead of 500,
- storing each vector in 48 bytes instead of 1,536, and scoring it with 48 table lookups,
- clustering the index so a search downloads a few hundred kilobytes, not hundreds of megabytes,
- and adding concept tags when pure semantic similarity started matching people on generic words.

Part 2 covers the data pipeline and storage. Part 3 covers matching, the tags and the test set.

### Academic Matchmaker, part 2: Fitting 181,568 researchers into a static website

https://someshmohapatra.in/writing/academic-matchmaker/storage-and-data-pipeline/ · 2026-10-28
